strengths: The paper addresses a very important and timely question in geometric deep learning: when does distributional symmetry breaking (where the input data density is not invariant under group transformations) affect the performance of equivariant models and data augmentation?

The proposed task-independent metric $m(p_X)$ is simple, elegant, and highly practical. Using a two-sample neural classifier test sidesteps the challenging kernel selection required by MMD and yields an easily interpretable score between 50% and 100%.

The theoretical analysis of invariant ridge regression under distributional asymmetry is rigorous and highly informative, using random matrix theory to show that data augmentation can indeed be harmful in the over-parameterized regime when invariant and non-invariant features are strongly correlated.

The empirical discovery that many standard benchmark datasets (such as QM9, ModelNet40, rMD17, OC20, and even LLM text-based molecular representations) are heavily canonicalized is highly significant for the community.

The paper does a great job of diagnosing the counterintuitive success of equivariant models on globally canonicalized datasets (like QM9) by introducing the concept of local symmetry/motifs, demonstrating that local neighborhoods are much more isotropic than the global structures.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are limited to linear (ridge) regression. While this is standard for tractable high-dimensional analysis (e.g., NTK limits), there is still a gap between this linear setting and the highly non-linear, deep architectures used in practice.

The task-dependent metric is less robust than the task-independent one, showing high sensitivity to the choice of canonicalization and classifier architectures, and yielding somewhat inconclusive results on complex real-world datasets.

Some of the key definitions and discussions (especially regarding the task-dependent metric and the direct prediction metric) are briefly introduced in the main text and rely heavily on the reader consulting the appendix for clarity.

The concept of 'secret canonicalization' in point clouds and molecular datasets has been discussed or implicitly utilized in previous works (e.g., noting that SMILES strings or molecular coordinates are generated in a standardized alignment), although this work is the first to measure and quantify it systematically via a classifier test.

strengths: Important and timely research question: The paper critically evaluates the implicit assumption of uniform group orbit distributions in equivariant machine learning and data augmentation, introducing the concept of distributional symmetry breaking.

Simple and intuitive metric: The proposed two-sample neural classifier test for measuring symmetry breaking is elegant, easy to implement, and directly interpretable (accuracy between 50% and 100%), avoiding kernel selection issues of previous MMD-based tests.

Strong theoretical support: The authors provide a rigorous high-dimensional ridge/ridgeless regression analysis under distributional symmetry breaking, demonstrating that data augmentation can indeed be detrimental when invariant and non-invariant features are strongly correlated.

Extensive empirical findings: Probes several standard point cloud datasets (QM9, rMD17, OC20, ModelNet40) and reveals that they are secretly highly canonicalized. Explores the counterintuitive phenomenon of why data augmentation still helps on molecular datasets by demonstrating that local motifs are much less canonicalized.
weaknesses: The theoretical model is restricted to linear/ridge regression. While this can model wide neural networks in the NTK regime, it may not fully capture the active representation learning dynamics of deep neural networks.

The task-dependent metric proposed in Section 5.2 appears to be highly sensitive to the choice of the classifier and canonicalization network architectures, as noted by the authors in Table 2 and Table 3. This limits its immediate practical applicability.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and overlooked issue in symmetry-aware machine learning: the implicit assumption that group transformations of data are uniformly distributed under the data-generating distribution.

The proposed metric $m(p_X)$ for measuring distributional symmetry-breaking is simple, elegant, highly interpretable, and computationally practical, bypassing the need for complex hand-designed kernels used in prior MMD-based statistical tests.

The theoretical analysis under the high-dimensional linear regression framework is technically rigorous and provides clear insights, showing that strong correlation between invariant and non-invariant features can make data augmentation detrimental in the over-parameterized regime.
The empirical finding that popular benchmarks like QM9, rMD17, and ModelNet40 are highly canonicalized (i.e., globally anisotropic) is surprising and critical for the community.

The explanation of the discrepancy between datasets (e.g., why augmentation helps on QM9 but hurts on ModelNet40) via local motif isotropy vs. global canonicalization is highly insightful and backed by solid experiments.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with high-quality figures, comprehensive literature positioning, and a thorough 71-page appendix detailing all proofs and experimental setups.
weaknesses: The proposed task-dependent metric (Section 5.2) is less robust than the task-independent one, showing high sensitivity to the choice of canonicalization and classifier architectures as shown in the ablation studies.

The theoretical analysis is restricted to linear ridge regression in the high-dimensional limit. While this is a standard proxy for neural networks in the lazy regime, extending these insights to deep representation learning remains an open challenge.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored assumption in equivariant representation learning and data augmentation: the assumption of distributional symmetry (isotropy).

Proposes a simple, practical, and model-agnostic metric ($m(p_X)$) based on classifier two-sample tests, avoiding the need for domain-specific kernels and making it widely applicable across different modalities (point clouds, graphs, text, images).
Provides a rigorous and novel theoretical analysis of invariant ridge regression under asymmetric data distributions, clearly showing how feature correlations can make data augmentation harmful.
Uncovers massive symmetry biases (canonicalization) in popular benchmark datasets (QM9, ModelNet40, OC20, rMD17).

Nicely resolves the mystery of why data augmentation behaves differently on different canonicalized datasets by introducing a task-dependent metric $t(p_{X,Y})$ and showing that local neighborhoods in molecules are much more isotropic than global structures.
weaknesses: The description of the task-dependent metric $t(p_{X,Y})$ in the main text is quite brief and could be made more intuitive for readers who do not dive into the appendix.

The theoretical analysis, while valuable, is restricted to linear/ridge regression settings with a simplified covariance model; extending these insights to deep non-linear networks remains a challenge.
Practical guidelines or architectural remedies for handling the detected symmetry breaking (beyond the selective augmentation heuristic explored in the appendix) are somewhat limited.

strengths: Important and Timely Topic: The paper systematically studies distributional symmetry breaking (symmetry bias in datasets), a crucial but often overlooked aspect in geometric deep learning where most papers assume isotropic data distributions.

Simple and General Metric: The proposed classifier-based metric $m(p_X)$ is highly practical, domain-agnostic, and avoids the complex kernel design issues of MMD-based statistical tests, making it easily applicable to images, point clouds, molecules, and text.

Strong Theoretical Foundation: The theoretical analysis of high-dimensional ridge regression (both under- and over-parameterized regimes) under non-symmetric covariance is excellent. It formally proves that data augmentation can be suboptimal or harmful even when the ground-truth function is invariant, especially when invariant and non-invariant features are strongly correlated.

Rich Empirical Insights: The discovery that common molecular benchmarks (QM9, QM7b) are highly canonicalized/oriented is eye-opening. The paper successfully resolves the mystery of why equivariant models still work well on these biased molecular datasets by showing that (a) the bias is not task-predictive for most properties, and (b) local motifs are much more isotropic than the global structures.
weaknesses: Heuristic Thresholds: While the flowchart in Figure 6 is practically useful, the thresholds for the metrics (e.g., whether $t(p_{X,Y}) \gg 1$) are mostly heuristic and lack a systematic or theoretical way to be determined, which might limit the immediate plug-and-play usability of the diagnostic tool.

Simplified Theoretical Assumptions: The theoretical analysis in the over-parameterized regime (Theorem 2) relies on a very specific, simplified covariance structure (coupling modes with perfect superpositions) to maintain tractability. It remains an open question how well this minimal model translates to complex neural network representations in practice.

Lack of Downstream Verification for Locality Hypothesis: In Section 5.2, the authors show that local motifs are less canonicalized than global ones, which is a great insight. However, the connection back to the downstream regression task is purely qualitative. It would strengthen the paper to show empirically whether a purely local equivariant model indeed outperforms a global equivariant model when local motifs are isotropic but global ones are canonicalized.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important but frequently neglected assumption in geometric deep learning and data augmentation: that the data distribution is uniform over group orbits (distributional symmetry). Exploring the consequences of violating this assumption is a timely and significant contribution.
The proposed classifier-based metric $m(p_X)$ is simple, highly intuitive, and practically robust, effectively avoiding the difficult kernel selection problems of prior MMD-based tests.

The theoretical analysis of high-dimensional ridge regression under non-symmetric covariance is mathematically rigorous. It clearly demonstrates that data augmentation can be detrimental in the over-parameterized regime when invariant and non-invariant features are strongly correlated, even when the ground-truth function is invariant.

The empirical evaluation is exceptionally thorough, spanning multiple domains (computer vision, point clouds, molecular property prediction, and even material LLMs) and analyzing why equivariance behaves differently across these datasets via task-dependent and local symmetry metrics.

The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear visualizations, an intuitive flowchart (Figure 6), and an extensive appendix containing complete proofs, extensive ablations, and reproducibility details.
weaknesses: The theoretical insights are established in the linear ridge regression and NTK regimes. While highly valuable, bridging the gap between these simplified settings and the non-linear feature learning dynamics of deep neural networks remains an open challenge.

The metric $m(p_X)$ requires training a classifier on the dataset. While the authors demonstrate that small networks are sufficient, this still introduces a non-trivial computational overhead compared to closed-form or non-parametric statistics on very large datasets.

The task-dependent metric $t(p_{X,Y})$ relies on a canonicalization function $c(x)$, implemented via a small equivariant network. As shown in the appendix (Tables 6 and 7), the metric exhibits some sensitivity to the architecture and optimization of this canonicalization network, which may complicate its black-box application.
